trade: Maths class with the school garden crew sizing a rain garden — learner and garden crew lead
header: Upper-primary maths at the Sunset District School Campus in San Francisco: how to measure a rain garden bed with a tape and a grid, find its length, width and area, and scale it on paper, using only what the tape, the grid and the garden in the scene show.
name: Measure a Rain Garden
tagline: Length times width gives the area — measure the bed with the crew, then draw it to scale

badge.name: Garden Measurer
badge.note: Measured a rain garden bed with a tape, worked out its area on a grid and drew it to scale for the crew

hazards.label: Add the length and width to get the area?
hazards.text: You added the length and the width. Adding them gives half the distance round the edge, not the area. Area counts the squares inside, so multiply the length by the width.

hazards.label: Start measuring from the end of the tape case?
hazards.text: You started from the tape case instead of the zero mark. The zero is at the hook end. Hold the hook on the edge of the bed and read where the other edge meets the tape.

hazards.label: Stretch the tape across the busy path?
hazards.text: You stretched the tape across the path where people walk. A tape at ankle height is a tripping line. Ask the crew lead to hold people back, and measure quickly, then reel it in.

hazards.label: Step into the bed to hold the tape?
hazards.text: You stepped into the garden bed. Feet pack the soil hard so it cannot soak up rain. Hold the tape from the path edge, and let the stakes mark the corners.

find1.title: Find what you need to measure
find1.cue: Mark the three things that tell you the size of the bed.
find1.why: To size a rectangle-shaped bed you need its length, its width and a way to see its corners. The corner stakes show where the bed begins and ends, the long side is the length, and the short side is the width. Once you have those, you can find the area and draw it on paper.
items: They mark where the bed ends.
the long side of the bed
the short side of the bed
decoy: Useful for watering, but not for measuring.

select1.title: Check the tape starts at zero
select1.cue: Point to the zero mark at the hook end of the tape before you start.
select1.why: Every measurement starts from zero. The hook end of the tape is the zero mark, so it goes on the edge you measure from. Checking it first stops a very common mistake, and crews check it every time before they cut or dig.
select1.label: Zero checked

seq.title: Put the measuring steps in order
seq.cue: Put the steps for finding the bed's area in order.
seq.why: Finding an area has a clear order. You measure the length, measure the width, multiply them, and write the answer with its unit. Following the order means nothing gets missed and anyone can check your working.
seq.oon: Out of order. Measure the length first.
items: write the answer with square units

turn.title: Set the scale on the drawing grid
turn.cue: Turn the scale dial so one grid square stands for one step of the tape.
turn.why: A scale drawing uses small squares on paper to stand for real distances. Choosing the scale first means every side of the drawing matches the real bed. Garden planners draw to scale so they can plan plants before anyone digs.
turn.label: Drawing scale

gauge.title: Read the length on the tape
gauge.cue: Commit when the marker sits where the far stake meets the tape.
gauge.why: Reading the tape exactly where the far stake stands gives the true length. Read straight down, not from the side, so the line you see is the right one. A careful reading here makes the area correct later.
gauge.label: Tape reading
gauge.miss: Not at the far stake. Read where the stake meets the tape.

hold.title: Hold the tape hook on the corner stake
hold.cue: Hold the hook against the corner stake while your partner reads the tape.
hold.why: If the hook slips, the reading is too short. Holding it firmly against the stake keeps zero exactly on the corner. Measuring is a two-person job, one holding and one reading, just as the crew does it.
hold.brk: The hook slipped off the stake. Hold it on the corner again.
hold.label: Hold the hook

drag.title: Place the bed on the drawing grid
drag.cue: Drag the bed outline onto the grid so its corners sit on grid points.
drag.why: Putting the corners on grid points makes the scale drawing accurate. Then you can count the squares inside to check your multiplying. When the count and the sum match, you know your area is right.
drag.label: Bed outline
drag.miss: Not on the grid points yet. Line the corners up with the grid.

find2.title: Spot the parts to add to the plan
find2.cue: Look at the real garden and mark each part the plan should show.
find2.why: A good plan shows more than the edges. The kerb gap where water enters, the low middle where water collects and the path around the bed all matter to the crew. Adding them helps the crew plant the right things in the right places.
items: the kerb gap where water enters
Show where the water comes in.
the low middle of the bed
decoy: Rain may come from it, but it does not go on the plan.

select2.title: Choose the right area sum
select2.cue: Choose the sum that gives the area of the bed.
select2.why: The area of a rectangle is its length multiplied by its width. A sum that adds them gives part of the distance round the edge instead. Choosing the multiply sum shows you know the difference between area and perimeter.
select2.label: Area sum

track.title: Trace the edge of the bed on the grid
track.cue: Keep the marker on the edge as you trace all the way round the bed.
track.why: Tracing the edge shows the perimeter, the distance all the way round. It is different from the area, which is the space inside. Tracing both on the same drawing helps you see why they are measured differently.
track.brk: The marker left the edge. Find the edge again and keep tracing.
track.label: Edge traced

record.title: Record the measurements and the area
record.cue: Write the length, the width and the area with their units on the plan.
record.why: Writing every measurement with its unit lets anyone check your work. The crew uses these numbers to order soil and plants. A missing unit can cause a big mix-up, so units always go with the numbers.
record.label: Measurement record

share.title: Check your area with another pair
share.cue: Compare your area with another pair who measured the same bed.
share.why: Two pairs measuring the same bed should get about the same answer. If not, someone may have missed zero or added instead of multiplied. Checking with others is how crews catch mistakes before they order materials.
share.label: Compare areas

checkin.title: Check in before handing the plan over
checkin.cue: How do you find the area of the bed? Why do units matter?
checkin.why: The crew lead checks the plan before using it, and the class checks its understanding too. Each learner explains length times width and why units go with numbers. If anyone added instead of multiplying, the group sorts it out now.
checkin.label: End-of-lesson check-in

interrupts.label: Lower the tape and wait
interrupts.alert: A classmate walks along the path towards the stretched tape.
interrupts.cue: Lower the tape to the ground and wait for them to pass.
interrupts.why: A stretched tape is easy to trip over. Lowering it to the ground and waiting lets people pass safely. Crews do the same with any line or hose across a path.
interrupts.miss: The tape stayed stretched, and the classmate had to stop short before stepping over it.
interrupts.wrong: That leaves the tape stretched across the path. Lower it. Choose the response that deals with it now.
interrupts.done: Tape lowered, the path clear. The lesson carries on.

interrupts.label: Say how to find the area
interrupts.alert: The crew lead asks how you will work out the area.
interrupts.cue: Say you multiply the length by the width and write square units.
interrupts.why: Knowing the rule shows you can plan the garden. The area tells the crew how much soil and how many plants they need. Getting it right saves time and materials.
interrupts.miss: You could not say how to find the area, and the crew lead had to explain before the class went on.
interrupts.wrong: That does not give the area rule. Choose the response that deals with it now.
interrupts.done: Area rule explained. The lesson carries on.

guide.start: Start at zero, length then width.
guide.hazard: Stop. Tape low, feet out of the bed.

lateRecord: The measurements are written once you have read the tape — nothing to record yet.
lateCheckin: The check-in comes at the very end of the lesson.
